pages.text: A [[matrix]] is a grid of numbers in rows and columns. This one has 2 rows and 3 columns, so it is a 2 by 3 grid. Each number is an [[entry]], named by its row first, then its column.

pages.name: Equations as a grid
pages.text: Take `x + 3y = 7` and `2x + y = 4`. Each equation's numbers make one row of the grid `[1 3; 2 1]`. The unknowns stand in a column beside it, and the totals in a column after the equals sign. To read a row back, multiply across it and down the unknowns, then add.

pages.name: Which grid?
pages.why: Row 1 holds the numbers of `3x + 2y`, which are 3 and 2. Row 2 holds the numbers of `x − y`, which are 1 and −1. So the grid is `[3 2; 1 −1]`.

pages.name: Columns are arrows
pages.text: Read down its columns, and the grid is two arrows, `(1, 2)` and `(3, 1)`. The grid times `(2, 1)` takes 2 lots of column 1 and 1 lot of column 2, nose to tail. Two lots of `(1, 2)` reach `(2, 4)`, and one `(3, 1)` more lands on `(5, 5)`.

pages.name: Rows and columns
pages.text: Row 1 holds the top number of each column. That is each arrow's across part. So row 1 adds the across parts of the chain, and it reads `x + 3y = 6`. Row 2 adds the up parts, and it reads `2x + y = 7`. Each column is one arrow, and moving its tip changes the grid's numbers.

pages.task: In `[2 4; 1 3]`, which pair is row 2 as an equation and column 2 as an arrow?
pages.why: Row 2 runs across, through 1 and 3, so it reads `x + 3y`. Column 2 runs down, through 4 and 3, so it is the arrow `(4, 3)`.

pages.name: Hit the target
pages.text: To land on the target `(7, 4)`, the across parts must make 7 and the up parts 4. That is `x + 3y = 7` and `2x + y = 4`, the same pair as before. Together they are [[simultaneous equations]]. One lot of column 1 and two of column 2 hit the target.

pages.name: Aim for (9, 8)
pages.task: Which equations find the amounts that hit `(9, 8)`?
pages.why: Row 1 adds the across parts, `x + 3y`, and the target is 9 across. Row 2 adds the up parts, `2x + y`, and it is 8 up. They give `x = 3` and `y = 2`. Not every target can be hit. Two arrows along one line reach only points on that line.

pages.name: How big?
pages.task: What size is the grid for `x + y = 5`, `x − y = 1` and `2x + y = 8`?
pages.why: Three equations make 3 rows. Two unknowns, `x` and `y`, make 2 columns. Rows come first, so it is a 3 by 2 grid. Turning its rows into columns gives its [[transpose]], a 2 by 3 grid. A grid with as many rows as columns is [[square]].

pages.name: Loop currents
pages.task: An example circuit's two loops give the grid `[6 −2; −2 6]` in ohms. It times the loop currents to give each loop's voltage. Which column of voltages do currents of 2.5 A and 1.5 A give?
pages.why: Row 1 gives `6 × 2.5 − 2 × 1.5 = 12`. Row 2 gives `−2 × 2.5 + 6 × 1.5 = 4`. So the voltages are 12 V and 4 V, and `6I₁ − 2I₂ = 12` and `−2I₁ + 6I₂ = 4` both hold.
